title: Trinity Sunday
hookLine: the Sunday after Pentecost is about who God is

lines: AN ANSWER TRACED ON YOUR BODY.
cards: Christmas, Good Friday, Easter, Pentecost: each remembers something that happened, a birth, a death, a rising, a wind in a room. Trinity Sunday is different. Nothing happened on it.
No event, no saint, no story. The week after Pentecost, having walked through the whole year of what God did, the Church stops and asks the question underneath all of it: who is God?
A child raised Catholic is handed the answer before they have words for it, each time an adult traces a cross over them.

teach.h: THE WORD ISN'T IN THE BIBLE.
teach.b: Here's a surprise first: the word Trinity isn't in the Bible. What's there is a pattern.

At the end of Matthew, the risen Jesus sends the apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice it says the name, singular, then three.
Paul ends a letter to Corinth with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost.
Early Christians found themselves praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and needed words for what they were already doing.

A writer in North Africa named Tertullian, arguing against a teacher called Praxeas, used the Latin trinitas, a threeness. Later, the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople gave the Creed Catholics still say on Sunday.
The Church's teaching is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks.
The Church calls it a mystery, which in its language doesn't mean a puzzle to give up on.

teach.h: A MYSTERY TO GO DEEPER INTO.
teach.b: It means something true that you can keep going deeper into forever. The feast itself spread slowly through the Middle Ages, until a pope put it on the calendar of the whole Church.

There's a well-known story that Saint Patrick explained the Trinity with a shamrock. It's lovely, and it's a later legend; his own writings don't mention it. What Catholics actually do every day is simpler.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: They touch forehead, chest and both shoulders, and say the name.

how: On the Sunday after Pentecost Catholics celebrate Trinity Sunday, wearing white at Mass and professing the Creed; every day Catholics mark themselves with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

o: a feast of three great saints together
the Sunday the Creed was first written
a feast of one God in three persons

s: the word Trinity appears in the Bible
the pattern is there, Father, Son and Spirit, but the word came later, in Tertullian's Latin.
in Catholic teaching, a mystery means a puzzle to give up on
it means something true you can keep going deeper into.
Matthew's baptism line says the name, singular, then three
in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

games.q: a friend asks you to sum up the Church's teaching on God in one line. which matches the Creed?
o: three gods who work as a team.
one God who wears three masks.
one God in three persons, each fully God.
games.why: one God in three persons. the early Church rejected both three gods and one God taking turns in three roles.

practice: Make the sign of the cross three times, slowly: the first at your usual speed, noticing how quickly it's over; the second pausing at each touch, forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder; the third letting each name take a whole breath.
If you're not someone who makes the sign, simply sit and notice your breath going in, resting, going out.

wordCard.voice: Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, a feast of the mystery of one God in three persons. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: threeness, a trinity; used by Tertullian.

carryVoice: Your line: one god, three persons. Forehead, chest, one shoulder, then the other. That's six hundred seventy-one.
